text: Good afternoon everyone.
My name is Estevão.
I am from Brazil.
This is my first time in the UK.
It's a pleasure to be here with you today.
So, let me tell you a little about my work.
I work at Motriz.
We are an NGO that supports more than 40 municipalities and seven state governments across Brazil.
Together we reach around three million students and 200,000 teachers.
Basically, our mission is to support governments in strengthening the public education system to improve learning outcomes and reduce educational inequalities.
So let me tell you about the challenge in Brazil.
Brazil has a huge education system with 47 million students, 179,000 schools, and 2.4 million teachers, and with more than 5,500 municipalities.
So governments need to implement policies across very different contexts and at a very large scale.
Over the past few years, Brazil has made important progress in education.
For example, learning is advancing at every stage of education, but one challenge still remains.
A study by Olavano Gerafilio right here at Oxford shows something important.
Large education systems in Brazil improve more slowly than smaller ones.
So the question is: how can large public education systems turn policy into better learning outcomes?
Well, over the past 10 years, we have learned that one of the biggest challenges in large education systems in Brazil is not policy design; it's policy implementation.
Implementation is the bridge between policy and what happens in schools.
And that's exactly where Motriz works.
We support governments in building strong implementation infrastructure.
Today I will show our work and some lessons that we have learned over these past few years.
Let me start with the most common implementation we have seen in Brazil in large public education systems.
In Brazil, there's usually one central education department, some regional education departments (the middle tier), and schools.
At Motriz, we call this model the waterfall model.
It's a top-down model focused on commands and control.
Decisions are made by a small group of leaders at the top and flow down to the system.
Schools and regional departments—the middle tier—have little voice in decision-making, and there's little room to listen, learn, or adapt policies to local needs.
From our experience over the past few years, we have learned that better implementation requires every level of the education system to work together.
We don't believe in only top-down or only bottom-up implementation; we believe the key is to keep every level connected.
At Motriz, we help governments build implementation systems based on feedback loops and collaboration.
We call this the pororoca model.
The pororoca is a special wave in the Amazon that happens when the Amazon River meets the Atlantic.
It forms a long, continuous, tube-shaped wave like this.
For us, it's a perfect symbol of a strong implementation system.
We focus on creating a system where every level learns from the others.
The central education department learns from regional departments.
Regional departments learn from schools.
The schools learn from each other.
Support moves down, feedback moves up, and learning moves in every direction.
This helps governments adapt policy to local needs and creates alignment across the whole system.
And importantly, to make this work, the central education department and regional teams need to work together and share responsibility for implementation.
That's how you build better implementation across the public education systems in Brazil.
So how do you move from the waterfall model to the pororoca model?
Let me give you an example: the government's pedagogical support policy.
We help governments build a central team of experienced education coaches, many of them former regional leaders or former school principals.
They regularly visit regional departments to support them and understand their challenges.
Regional teams also have experienced education coaches, many of them former school principals, who regularly visit schools.
They support school leaders, listen to local challenges, help analyze data, and develop action plans to turn policy into classroom practice.
After each school visit, the feedback goes back to the regional team.
The regional team analyzes information, plans action to support schools, and shares the information with the central education department.
Together they identify local challenges, adapt policies, and improve support for regional departments and schools.
And this creates a continuous feedback loop.
Support moves down, feedback moves up, and every level learns from the others.
Policies become stronger because they adapt to challenges on the ground.
From our experience in Brazil, frequent and consistent routines help strengthen the system and build trust, and importantly, it's not about inspection or punishment.
It's about continuous support and alignment at every level.
They help leaders collect and analyze data together, understand real challenges, and make better decisions.
At Motriz, we support governments in designing these feedback loops and continuously developing education coaches to carry out these visits.
To help governments track implementation progress, we create predictors of learning.
It's an evidence-based methodology developed by Motriz after years of studying how implementation can improve learning outcomes.
This methodology helps governments understand how policies are reaching schools and regional departments based on the perceptions of school principals and regional leaders.
So, how does it work?
We send a simple online survey to a sample of school principals and regional leaders.
We ask simple questions to understand how policies are working in schools and regional departments.
Based on the answers, we organize the results on a 0 to 10 scale and analyze them with education leaders.
This helps governments identify which policies need more attention and which ones are working well.
Leaders can see where more support is needed, identify outliers and positive deviants, and share good practices across the system.
This helps governments make better decisions and strengthen implementation.
The methodology also helps governments balance accountability and flexibility.
It creates accountability by helping leaders track implementation across the whole system but also gives them flexibility to adapt policies to local needs.
And importantly, we don't use data to compare municipalities or create rankings.
We only use it to help governments track progress, learn from the data, and adapt the policies to local needs over time.
We also create ways to directly listen to teachers and students.
Their voices are an important part of the feedback loop.
Today in Ceará, we are running a large survey with more than 15,000 teachers and 260,000 students.
We ask simple questions to understand how policies are working in schools and how we can better support teaching and learning.
This helps education leaders understand challenges in the classroom, adapt policy to local needs, and improve teaching and learning.
Let me give you a concrete example: one municipality created chess clubs to teach mathematics in a more practical and engaging way.
After the survey, education leaders found that students didn't like chess; they preferred music and visual arts.
So they replaced the chess clubs with music and arts clubs using practical mathematics.
The activity changed, but the goal stayed the same.
Students became much more engaged, and this made a real difference.
What we have learned is simple: listening to people on the ground leads to better implementation.
To finish, I would like to share the case of Rio de Janeiro, the largest municipal education system in Latin America.
It has more than 600,000 students, 55,000 education staff, 1,500 schools, and 11 regional education departments.
It also faces major challenges: around 30% of its schools are in neighborhoods affected by violence and criminal groups.
Even so, learning outcomes have improved significantly over the last few years.
When you look at the predictors of learning data in Rio, we can see that results are improving year after year.

This shows the growing maturity of the implementation process over time, and at the same time, when you look at learning outcomes, Rio de Janeiro also improves consistently across all stages over time.
In Rio, we see three key pillars behind this progress.
First, strong leadership at every level.
Leaders connect and engage teams, set clear goals, listen to people, and provide direction.
Second, strong pedagogical support.
The central team supports regional teams, and regional teams support schools.
They listen to challenges and bring feedback back to the system.
Some schools receive weekly visits from regional education departments.
This creates a continuous feedback loop and helps the system adapt to local needs.
And third, data.
Rio collects a lot of both quantitative and qualitative data to track implementation processes and learning outcomes.
The government works with universities, NGOs, and civil society organizations to strengthen implementation and help leaders and staff collect, systematize, organize, and use data.
This helps leaders identify what's working and what needs to improve.
These partnerships build state capacity and make change more sustainable.
So to close, I want to highlight three key lessons we have learned from our work with large education systems in Brazil.
First, build an implementation infrastructure with continuous feedback across every level.
We need to keep all levels of the system connected.
Second, use data to track implementation progress over time and learn what is working and what needs to change.
We need to collect, organize, and analyze both quantitative and qualitative data all the time.
And third, have strong leaders at every level to create alignment, provide direction, and engage staff around shared goals.
For us, success means strengthening the government's ability to listen, learn, and adapt so policies can improve over time and reach schools in practice.
Thank you very much.
